intro: SYNC Manufacturing provides custom rubber-to-metal bonding services for OEMs requiring durable, high-performance components that combine the structural strength of metal with the flexibility, resilience, and sealing properties of engineered elastomers.
Our capabilities include vulcanization bonding, compression molding, transfer molding, adhesive bonding, mechanical encapsulation, custom rubber compounding, and metal insert manufacturing.
Drawing upon decades of specialized manufacturing experience, SYNC produces bonded components for aerospace, defense, utilities, flow control, oil and gas, and industrial equipment applications.

From vibration isolators and industrial mounts to bonded valve assemblies, rubber-covered rollers, and custom seals, our engineering teams work with customers to identify the appropriate materials, bonding methods, and manufacturing processes.

blocks.text: Rubber-to-metal bonding is a manufacturing process that joins rubber or another compatible elastomer to a metal substrate to create an integrated component.
The metal provides structural strength, rigidity, and mechanical attachment, while the elastomer contributes flexibility, vibration damping, impact absorption, or sealing performance.
In a typical vulcanization bonding process, metal inserts are cleaned, prepared, and treated with a bonding system before uncured rubber is molded against the substrate.
During molding, heat and pressure cure the elastomer while the bonding system develops adhesion between the rubber and metal.
The resulting assembly combines the functional advantages of both materials into a single engineered component.
Depending on part design and application requirements, other approaches may include post-cure adhesive bonding or mechanical encapsulation.
Advantages of Rubber-to-Metal Bonding
Integrated Component Design
Combining rubber and metal into one assembly can reduce separate components, simplify installation, and eliminate certain secondary assembly steps.
Vibration & Shock Absorption
Engineered elastomers can reduce vibration transmission, absorb mechanical energy, and protect sensitive industrial equipment.
Sealing Performance
Bonded rubber surfaces can provide durable sealing interfaces while retaining the structural support of the metal component.
Mechanical Strength & Flexibility
The combination of metal and rubber allows components to accommodate mechanical loads, deformation, and repeated movement.
Material Customization
Rubber compounds and bonding systems can be selected to meet application-specific mechanical, thermal, and environmental requirements.
Long-Term Reliability
Controlled surface preparation, material selection, bonding chemistry, and molding conditions help support consistent adhesion and component durability.
SYNC offers several bonding and molding processes to accommodate different materials, part geometries, production volumes, and performance requirements.
Vulcanization Bonding
Vulcanization bonding chemically joins uncured rubber to a prepared metal substrate during the molding process.
An appropriate bonding system is applied to the metal insert before the rubber is molded and cured.
The bonding system, elastomer compound, and processing conditions are selected to develop adhesion that meets the intended service requirements.
This method is commonly used for components requiring strong adhesion under mechanical loading, vibration, or repeated deformation.
Compression Molded Bonded Assemblies
Compression molding uses heat and pressure to form rubber around prepared metal inserts.
This process can be particularly effective for larger components, substantial cross sections, industrial mounts, valve parts, and specialized bonded assemblies.
Transfer Molded Bonded Components
Transfer molding moves uncured elastomer into a closed mold containing prepared metal inserts.
The process can offer advantages for complex geometries, intricate details, multiple inserts, and components requiring controlled material placement.
Adhesive Bonding
Certain applications are better suited to joining previously cured elastomer components to metal using specialized adhesive systems.
The selected adhesive must be compatible with the rubber compound, metal substrate, operating conditions, and required bond performance.
Mechanical Encapsulation
Mechanical encapsulation uses component geometry to retain rubber around or within a metal insert.
This method may involve grooves, undercuts, or other interlocking features and can be used independently or alongside chemical adhesion, depending on design requirements.

The performance of a rubber-to-metal bonded component begins with selecting the correct elastomer compound.
SYNC's in-house rubber compounding expertise supports specialized formulations for demanding mechanical and environmental applications.
Common Elastomer Materials
Natural Rubber (NR)
Excellent resilience, elasticity, and dynamic performance for vibration isolation and mechanical components.
EPDM
Resistance to ozone, weathering, water, and many outdoor environmental conditions.
Nitrile Rubber (NBR)
Suitable for applications requiring compatibility with selected petroleum-based oils, fuels, and lubricants.
Neoprene (CR)
Balanced mechanical properties with useful resistance to weathering and selected industrial environments.
Silicone Rubber (VMQ)
Flexibility over a broad temperature range, environmental aging resistance, and selected electrical properties.
Styrene-Butadiene Rubber (SBR)
A versatile compound for general industrial components requiring mechanical durability and abrasion resistance.
Fluoroelastomers (FKM)
Used in demanding applications involving elevated temperatures and selected aggressive chemicals or fluids.
Specialty Elastomers
Additional formulations, including HNBR, butyl rubber, urethane elastomers, and other engineered compounds, may be considered depending on application and bonding requirements.

Successful rubber-to-metal bonding requires careful coordination throughout the manufacturing process.
1. Engineering & Material Selection
Our engineering teams review component geometry, mechanical loads, service conditions, metal substrates, and elastomer requirements.
These considerations help determine the appropriate rubber formulation, bonding method, and molding process.
2. Metal Surface Preparation
The metal substrate is prepared to promote reliable adhesion.
Depending on the material and bonding system, surface preparation may include cleaning, degreasing, abrasive treatment, and other controlled processes.
3. Bonding System Application
Specialized primers, adhesives, or other bonding systems are applied to prepared metal surfaces as appropriate.
Application methods and process parameters are selected for the particular substrate and elastomer combination.
4. Molding & Vulcanization
Prepared metal components are placed into the tooling.
Uncured rubber is molded around or against the inserts using the selected compression or transfer molding process.
Heat and pressure cure the rubber and develop adhesion between the elastomer and metal substrate.
5. Finishing & Inspection
Finished components undergo appropriate trimming, finishing, and inspection.
Depending on customer requirements, quality verification may include visual inspection, dimensional measurements, material-property testing, and adhesion evaluation.

a.text: Rubber-to-metal bonding joins elastomer materials to metal substrates to create integrated components combining the properties of both materials.

faq.q: How is rubber bonded to metal?

a.text: Common methods include chemical bonding during vulcanization, adhesive bonding of previously cured rubber, and mechanical encapsulation.

faq.q: What metals can be bonded to rubber?

a.text: Common substrates include steel, stainless steel, aluminum, and brass. Other metals may be evaluated depending on the bonding system and application.

faq.q: Which rubber materials can be bonded to metal?

a.text: Natural rubber, nitrile, EPDM, neoprene, silicone, SBR, and specialized elastomers can be used in appropriate bonding applications.

faq.q: Can rubber-to-metal bonding withstand heavy mechanical loads?

a.text: Properly engineered bonded components can be designed for demanding mechanical applications. Performance depends on rubber formulation, bond design, substrate preparation, service conditions, and manufacturing controls.

faq.q: Can SYNC use customer-supplied metal inserts?

a.text: Yes. SYNC can evaluate customer-supplied metal inserts based on material, dimensional, surface preparation, and manufacturing requirements.

faq.q: Does SYNC offer custom rubber compounding?

a.text: Yes. SYNC has in-house rubber compounding expertise to support specialized mechanical, chemical, thermal, and environmental requirements.

faq.q: Can SYNC support existing tooling and production transfers?

a.text: Yes. Our manufacturing teams can review existing tooling, drawings, material specifications, and production requirements to determine an appropriate transfer strategy.
